name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_STATEMENTBASED3_Q01 - Properties of Group 15 hydrides and nitrogen

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements carefully regarding Group 15 elements and their compounds:

Statement I: The thermal stability of Group 15 hydrides decreases from \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) to \(\mathrm{BiH}_3\), which results in an increase in their reducing character down the group.

Statement II: \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) has a higher boiling point than \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) because \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding in the liquid state.

Statement III: Nitrogen forms pentahalides such as \(\mathrm{NCl}_5\) by expanding its covalency beyond four using vacant \(d\)-orbitals.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The properties of Group 15 elements and their hydrides are governed by atomic size, electronegativity, \(\mathrm{E}-\mathrm{H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy, and the availability of valence-shell \(d\)-orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation of Thermal Stability and Reducing Character of Hydrides
As we move down Group 15 from \(\mathrm{N}\) to \(\mathrm{Bi}\), the atomic size increases and the \(\mathrm{E}-\mathrm{H}\) bond length increases, causing the \(\mathrm{E}-\mathrm{H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy to decrease regularly from \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) to \(\mathrm{BiH}_3\). Consequently, thermal stability decreases down the group, and the ease of liberating hydrogen increases. Therefore, the reducing character increases from \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) (a mild reducing agent) to \(\mathrm{BiH}_3\) (the strongest reducing agent among Group 15 hydrides). Thus, the claim regarding thermal stability and reducing character is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Boiling Points of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{PH}_3\)
Due to the small atomic size and high electronegativity of nitrogen, \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds in both solid and liquid states. In contrast, phosphorus has a larger size and lower electronegativity, so \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) molecules are not associated through hydrogen bonding. As a result, \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) has a significantly higher boiling point (\(238.5\ \mathrm{K}\)) than \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) (\(185.5\ \mathrm{K}\)). Thus, the claim regarding the boiling point of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Pentahalide Formation by Nitrogen
Nitrogen belongs to the second period (\(n = 2\)), so its valence shell contains only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals, with no \(d\)-orbitals available. Because only four orbitals are available for bonding, nitrogen is restricted to a maximum covalency of 4 and cannot expand its octet to form pentahalides such as \(\mathrm{NCl}_5\). Thus, the claim that nitrogen forms pentahalides using vacant \(d\)-orbitals is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding the thermal stability and reducing character of Group 15 hydrides and the higher boiling point of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) due to hydrogen bonding are correct, whereas the claim regarding pentahalide formation by nitrogen is incorrect.

answer.text: All I, II, and III are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_STATEMENTBASED3_Q02 - Structure, basicity, and disproportionation of phosphorus oxoacids

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements carefully regarding the oxoacids of phosphorus:

Statement I: Hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\)) is a monobasic acid because it contains only one \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\) bond, while its two \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are not ionisable.

Statement II: The strong reducing property of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is due to the presence of two \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds directly attached to the phosphorus atom.

Statement III: On heating, orthophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\)) disproportionates to form orthophosphoric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\)) and phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In oxoacids of phosphorus, the central phosphorus atom is tetrahedrally surrounded by other atoms and always contains at least one \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{O}\) bond and one \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\) bond. The chemical properties such as basicity, reducing nature, and disproportionation depend on the nature of bonds attached to phosphorus and its oxidation state.

Step 2: Evaluation of Basicity of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\)
In oxoacids of phosphorus, only those hydrogen atoms that are attached to oxygen in \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\) groups are ionisable to give \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions and determine basicity. Hydrogen atoms bonded directly to phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds) are not ionisable. Hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\)) contains one \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{O}\) bond, one \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\) bond, and two \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds. Since it has only one ionisable \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\) group, it is monobasic. Thus, the claim regarding the monobasicity of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Reducing Property of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\)
Oxoacids of phosphorus that contain \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds exhibit strong reducing properties. Because \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) has two \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds directly attached to the phosphorus atom, it acts as a strong reducing agent (for example, reducing \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\) to metallic silver). Thus, the claim regarding the reducing property of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Disproportionation of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\)
In \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) (orthophosphorous acid), phosphorus is in the \(+3\) intermediate oxidation state. Oxoacids of phosphorus in the \(+3\) oxidation state tend to disproportionate into higher (\(+5\)) and lower (\(-3\)) oxidation states on heating according to the reaction:
\[4\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3 \rightarrow 3\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4 + \mathrm{PH}_3\]
Here, phosphorus in \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) (\(+3\)) is simultaneously oxidised to \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) (\(+5\)) and reduced to \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) (\(-3\)). Thus, the claim regarding the disproportionation of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All three claims—concerning the monobasicity of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\), the origin of its reducing character from \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds, and the thermal disproportionation of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) into \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{PH}_3\)—are correct.

answer.text: All I, II, and III are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_STATEMENTBASED3_Q03 - Oxidising power of halogens, interhalogens, and xenon fluorides

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements carefully regarding halogens, interhalogen compounds, and xenon fluorides:

Statement I: Fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine, yet \(\mathrm{F}_2\) is a stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) due to its low \(\mathrm{F}-\mathrm{F}\) bond dissociation enthalpy and high hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{F}^-\) ion.

Statement II: Interhalogen compounds of the type \(\mathrm{XX}'\) are less reactive than the constituent halogens \(\mathrm{X}_2\) (excluding \(\mathrm{F}_2\)) because the \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}'\) bond is stronger than the \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}\) bond.

Statement III: Partial hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) with water produces \(\mathrm{XeOF}_4\) and \(\mathrm{XeO}_2\mathrm{F}_2\), and this reaction is a redox process in which the oxidation state of xenon changes.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The oxidising power of halogens in aqueous solution depends on bond dissociation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, and hydration enthalpy. The reactivity of interhalogens depends on the relative strength of heteronuclear \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}'\) bonds versus homonuclear \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}\) bonds, while hydrolysis of xenon fluorides is governed by oxidation state conservation in non-redox reactions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Oxidising Power of \(\mathrm{F}_2\) vs \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)
Although fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-333\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) than chlorine (\(-349\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) due to interelectronic repulsions in its compact \(2p\) orbitals, \(\mathrm{F}_2\) has a much lower bond dissociation enthalpy (\(158.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) vs \(242.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)) and a much higher hydration enthalpy for \(\mathrm{F}^-\) (\(-515\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) vs \(-381\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\)). These two factors outweigh the lower electron gain enthalpy, making \(\mathrm{F}_2\) a stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\). Thus, the claim regarding the oxidising power of \(\mathrm{F}_2\) is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Reactivity of Interhalogen Compounds
In general, interhalogen compounds (\(\mathrm{XX}'\)) are more reactive than halogens (except fluorine) because the heteronuclear \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}'\) bond in interhalogens is weaker than the homonuclear \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}\) bond in halogens (excluding the \(\mathrm{F}-\mathrm{F}\) bond). Claiming that \(\mathrm{XX}'\) is less reactive because \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}'\) is stronger than \(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{X}\) reverses the actual bond-strength relationship. Thus, the claim regarding the reactivity of interhalogen compounds is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Partial Hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\)
Partial hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) gives xenon oxyfluorides according to the equations:
\[\mathrm{XeF}_6 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{XeOF}_4 + 2\mathrm{HF}\]
\[\mathrm{XeF}_6 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{XeO}_2\mathrm{F}_2 + 4\mathrm{HF}\]
In \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\), \(\mathrm{XeOF}_4\), and \(\mathrm{XeO}_2\mathrm{F}_2\), the oxidation state of xenon remains \(+6\) (with \(\mathrm{O}\) as \(-2\), \(\mathrm{F}\) as \(-1\), and \(\mathrm{H}\) as \(+1\)). Since no element undergoes a change in oxidation state, partial hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) is not a redox reaction. Thus, the claim that it is a redox process is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Only the claim explaining why \(\mathrm{F}_2\) is a stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) is correct, whereas the claims regarding interhalogen bond strength/reactivity and the redox nature of \(\mathrm{XeF}_6\) partial hydrolysis are incorrect.
